paper.title: SKIPJACK and KEA Algorithm Specifications (version 2.0), with the SP 800-17 known-answer tables
paper.venue: NIST, 1998 (not a journal paper; a government specification)

program.how: written for ounce-core from the algorithm description; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: SKIPJACK encrypts the all-zero block under each of the 80 single-bit keys to the 80 ciphertexts of SP 800-17 Appendix B Table 6 (80 of 80), and decrypting them returns the plaintext (80 of 80)
the F-table (transcribed from the specification's scanned page) is a permutation of 0..255 and F(0x7a) = 0xd6 as the specification's example states

expected_values_source.what: the 80 ciphertexts of Table 6 (variable key known-answer test) as transcribed in the Crypto++ test-vector file skipjack.txt (which cites SP 800-17 Table 6), cross-read against the SP 800-17 PDF text (OCR): 78 of the 78 rows whose OCR text was legible agree after mapping OCR confusions (O to 0, I and l to 1); 2 rows were not legible. The F-table and the stepping rules were read from the scanned specification PDF
expected_values_source.note: the specification is a scanned image, so the 256 F-table bytes were transcribed by eye from the rendered page and validated by the permutation property, the spec's F(7a) example and the 80 vectors. SP 800-17 prints keys and blocks as numbers, most significant byte first, while the specification labels bytes from 0; the byte reversal was fixed by the first vector and applied unchanged to all 80. Data copied as numbers; no code was copied

negative_control: built with SKIPJACK_COUNTER0=0 (step counter starts at 0 instead of 1), 0 of 80 vectors match and the program exits 1
not_checked: SP 800-17 Table 5 (variable plaintext) and the CBC vectors
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about the authors' hardware)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces the 80 published SP 800-17 SKIPJACK ciphertexts. It does not show anything about SKIPJACK's security. This is a NIST specification, not a refereed paper.
